title: Computer Abbreviations and Terminology
summary: The abbreviations that recur in bank exams, grouped and explained rather than just expanded: hardware and storage, data units, software and operating systems, networking, web and data formats, and the standards bodies, with the comparisons examiners like to test.
learningObjectives: Expand the common hardware, storage and data-unit abbreviations and say what each names.
Group the software, operating-system and networking abbreviations and give a one-line meaning for each.
Recall the web, data-format and standards abbreviations examiners repeat.
State the standard comparisons: RAM vs ROM, HDD vs SSD, LAN vs WAN, GUI vs CLI, TCP vs UDP, HTTP vs HTTPS.

blocks.title: How to learn these
blocks.markdown:
Bank exams ask a steady trickle of "expand this abbreviation" and "which of these is *not* an output device" questions. Rote expansion is not enough — you also need the one-line sense, because the wrong options are usually real terms placed in the wrong group.

Learn them in the groups below (hardware, units, software/OS, networking, web/data, standards). For each entry, be able to say the full form **and** finish the sentence "it is the thing that …".

blocks.title: Hardware, storage and data units
blocks.markdown:
| Abbr. | Full form | In one line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CPU | Central Processing Unit | executes instructions; the "brain" |
| ALU | Arithmetic Logic Unit | part of the CPU that does calculation and comparison |
| CU | Control Unit | part of the CPU that directs the other units |
| RAM | Random Access Memory | fast, volatile working memory; cleared on power-off |
| ROM | Read Only Memory | non-volatile memory holding start-up firmware |
| PROM / EPROM / EEPROM | (Erasable / Electrically Erasable) Programmable ROM | ROM that can be written once, or erased by UV, or erased electrically |
| HDD | Hard Disk Drive | magnetic spinning-platter storage; cheap, slower |
| SSD | Solid State Drive | flash storage; no moving parts, faster |
| USB | Universal Serial Bus | standard port/connector for peripherals and drives |
| GPU | Graphics Processing Unit | processor specialised for graphics and parallel work |
| BIOS / UEFI | Basic Input/Output System / Unified Extensible Firmware Interface | firmware that starts the hardware and loads the OS; UEFI is the modern replacement |

**Data units:** a **bit** is one 0/1; **8 bits = 1 byte**; a **nibble** is 4 bits. Then **KB → MB → GB → TB → PB**, each ×1024 in the binary convention (×1000 in the decimal one).

blocks.title: Software and operating systems
blocks.markdown:
| Abbr. | Full form | In one line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OS | Operating System | manages hardware and runs programs (Windows, Linux, Android) |
| GUI | Graphical User Interface | interact via windows, icons and a pointer |
| CLI | Command Line Interface | interact by typing text commands |
| kernel | (not an abbreviation) | the core of the OS, always in memory, closest to the hardware |
| API | Application Programming Interface | a defined way for one program to call another |
| IDE | Integrated Development Environment | an editor, compiler/runner and debugger in one app |
| SDK | Software Development Kit | tools and libraries for building software for a platform |
| GUI vs CLI | — | GUI is easier to learn; CLI is faster to script and automate |

blocks.title: Networking
blocks.markdown:
| Abbr. | Full form | In one line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LAN / MAN / WAN | Local / Metropolitan / Wide Area Network | a network within a building, a city, or spanning regions/countries |
| ISP | Internet Service Provider | the company that connects you to the Internet |
| IP | Internet Protocol (address) | the numeric address of a device on a network |
| TCP / UDP | Transmission Control Protocol / User Datagram Protocol | reliable ordered delivery / fast connectionless delivery |
| HTTP / HTTPS | HyperText Transfer Protocol (Secure) | fetch web pages / the same over an encrypted TLS connection |
| FTP | File Transfer Protocol | move files between a client and a server |
| DNS | Domain Name System | resolves a domain name to an IP address |
| DHCP | Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol | hands a device its IP address automatically |
| URL | Uniform Resource Locator | the full address of a web resource |
| VPN | Virtual Private Network | an encrypted tunnel over a public network |
| MAC address | Media Access Control address | a hardware address burnt into a network adapter |

blocks.title: Web, data formats and standards
blocks.markdown:
**Web and data formats:**

| Abbr. | Full form | In one line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTML / CSS | HyperText Markup Language / Cascading Style Sheets | page structure / page styling |
| XML / JSON | eXtensible Markup Language / JavaScript Object Notation | text formats for structured data exchange |
| SQL | Structured Query Language | the language for relational databases |
| CSV | Comma-Separated Values | plain-text tabular data |
| PDF | Portable Document Format | fixed-layout document format |

**Media formats:** JPEG/PNG/GIF (images — photo, lossless/transparency, simple animation), MP3/MP4 (audio / video container), ZIP (compressed archive).

**Standards bodies:** IEEE (engineering standards, e.g. Wi-Fi 802.11), ISO (international standards), W3C (web standards), ASCII and Unicode (character-encoding standards — Unicode covers virtually every script, ASCII only 128 characters).

blocks.title: The comparisons examiners test
blocks.markdown:
| Pair | Key difference |
| --- | --- |
| **RAM vs ROM** | RAM is volatile read/write working memory; ROM is non-volatile and normally read-only (start-up firmware). |
| **HDD vs SSD** | HDD stores on spinning magnetic platters — cheaper per GB, slower, moving parts. SSD uses flash — faster, silent, more shock-resistant. |
| **LAN vs WAN** | LAN covers a single site and is privately owned; WAN spans cities or countries and usually uses leased/telecom links. |
| **GUI vs CLI** | GUI: windows, icons, pointer — easy to learn. CLI: typed commands — faster to automate and script. |
| **TCP vs UDP** | TCP sets up a connection and guarantees ordered, error-checked delivery. UDP is connectionless and fast, with no delivery guarantee (used for streaming, DNS, games). |
| **HTTP vs HTTPS** | HTTPS is HTTP carried over TLS: encrypted and with a verified server certificate. |
| **Compiler vs interpreter** | A compiler translates the whole program to machine code once; an interpreter executes the source line by line each run. |

blocks.title: Quick revision
blocks.markdown:
- **Hardware:** CPU (ALU + CU), RAM (volatile), ROM (firmware), HDD (magnetic), SSD (flash), GPU (graphics), BIOS/UEFI (start-up firmware).
- **Units:** 8 bits = 1 byte; KB→MB→GB→TB→PB (×1024 binary).
- **Software/OS:** OS manages hardware; GUI (icons/pointer) vs CLI (typed commands); API (program-to-program interface), IDE, SDK.
- **Networking:** LAN/MAN/WAN by size; ISP connects you; TCP reliable vs UDP fast; DNS name→IP; DHCP assigns IP; VPN encrypted tunnel; MAC = hardware address.
- **Web and data formats:** HTML structure, CSS style, XML/JSON data exchange, SQL for databases, CSV tabular text, PDF fixed layout.
- **Standards:** IEEE, ISO, W3C; ASCII (128 chars) vs Unicode (nearly all scripts).

blocks.title: Practice
blocks.markdown:
Expand each and give a one-line meaning; then answer the last two.

1. EEPROM
2. DHCP
3. SDK
4. UDP
5. Which of these is volatile: RAM or ROM?
6. Which stores data on flash with no moving parts: HDD or SSD?
7. Which resolves `example.org` to an IP address: DNS or DHCP?
8. ASCII or Unicode — which can represent characters from almost every writing system?
searchKeywords: computer abbreviations practice expand eeprom dhcp sdk udp ram rom hdd ssd dns unicode

flashcards.back: RAM (Random Access Memory) is fast, volatile read/write working memory that is cleared on power-off. ROM (Read Only Memory) is non-volatile and normally read-only, holding start-up firmware.
HDD (Hard Disk Drive) stores on spinning magnetic platters — cheaper per GB, slower, has moving parts. SSD (Solid State Drive) uses flash memory — faster, silent, more shock-resistant.

flashcards.front: What are the ALU and CU, and where do they sit?
flashcards.back: Both are parts of the CPU. The ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) performs calculation and comparison; the CU (Control Unit) directs the other units and the flow of instructions.
flashcards.explanation: Registers and cache are the CPU's own fast storage.

flashcards.front: How many bits in a byte, and what is the order KB, MB, GB, TB?
flashcards.back: 8 bits = 1 byte (a nibble is 4 bits). Sizes go KB → MB → GB → TB → PB, each step ×1024 in the binary convention (×1000 decimal).
flashcards.explanation: A bit is a single 0 or 1.

flashcards.back: GUI (Graphical User Interface) — interact through windows, icons and a pointer; easy to learn. CLI (Command Line Interface) — type text commands; faster to script and automate.
flashcards.explanation: Both are ways to drive the same operating system.

flashcards.back: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) sets up a connection and guarantees ordered, error-checked delivery. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless and fast with no delivery guarantee — used for streaming, DNS and games.
An Application Programming Interface — a defined set of calls by which one program uses the features or data of another, without needing to know its internals.
flashcards.explanation: An SDK is the wider toolkit (libraries + tools) for building on a platform.

flashcards.back: ASCII encodes 128 characters (English letters, digits, basic punctuation, control codes). Unicode is a much larger standard covering virtually every writing system, with encodings such as UTF-8.
flashcards.explanation: UTF-8 is backward-compatible with ASCII for the first 128 code points.
